essentialQuestion.note: 'tài nguyên' (KEY_TERMS) for 'resources' is used here in the sense of time, money, food and skills. In everyday Vietnamese 'tài nguyên' means natural resources, so 'nguồn lực' may be better for these. A reviewer should decide, and the change would apply throughout this lesson.

learningGoal.note: 'nhu cầu thiết yếu' for 'needs' and 'mong muốn' for 'wants': my choice (not in KEY_TERMS). I avoided plain 'nhu cầu' because in Vietnamese it can also cover wants. Alternatives: nhu cầu cần thiết / điều muốn có, ước muốn. 'sự khan hiếm' for scarcity; 'chi phí cơ hội' for opportunity cost (standard economics term, but abstract for a 10-year-old).
learningGoal.source: Explain scarcity, needs, wants and opportunity cost using everyday examples.
learningGoal.back: Explain scarcity, essential needs, wishes and opportunity cost using everyday examples.

read.sections.0.heading.note: Long heading. 'Tài nguyên giúp con người đáp ứng nhu cầu thiết yếu và mong muốn' is the longer side of a heading; check if it should be shortened.
read.sections.0.heading.source: Resources help people meet needs and wants
read.sections.0.heading.back: Resources help people meet essential needs and wishes

read.sections.0.text.note: Key economics terms introduced here (tài nguyên, nhu cầu thiết yếu, mong muốn). Check that the definitions read naturally and a learner can tell need from want. The dì (maternal or paternal aunt: 'dì' is mother's younger sister; 'cô' is father's sister, 'mợ'/'thím' other aunts): 'dì' was chosen, but the English only says 'aunt', so check a neutral word such as 'dì' is acceptable.
read.sections.0.text.source: Every day, people make choices, from what to do after class to how a household uses its food, money or phone data. To make these choices, people use resources. A resource is anything useful that people have, such as time, money, food, water, tools or skills. People use resources to meet their needs and wants. A need is something you must have to live safely and stay healthy, such as food, clean water and a safe place to sleep. A want is something you would like to have but can live without. For example, Noor's aunt needs to buy rice and soap, but a new football is a want.
read.sections.0.text.back: Every day, everyone has to make choices, from what to do after school to how a family uses food, money or phone data. To choose, people use resources. A resource is any useful thing people have, like time, money, food, water, tools or skills. People use resources to meet their essential needs and wishes. An essential need is something you must have in order to live safely and stay healthy, like food, clean water and a safe place to sleep. A wish is something you like to have but can still live if you lack it. For example, Noor's aunt needs to buy rice and soap, while a new football is a wish.

read.sections.0.simpler.note: Check it keeps the same ideas and is simple enough. 'Thiếu nó bạn vẫn sống được' for 'You can live without it'.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: People make choices every day. To choose, they use resources. A resource is something useful that you have. Time, money, food and skills are resources. A need is something you must have to live and stay well. A want is something you would like. You can live without it. Noor's aunt needs rice and soap. A new football is a want.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Every day everyone has to choose. To choose, people use resources. A resource is a useful thing you have. Time, money, food and skills are all resources. An essential need is something you must have to live and be healthy. A wish is something you like to have. Lacking it, you can still live. Noor's aunt needs to buy rice and soap. A new football is a wish.

read.sections.1.text.note: 'Sự khan hiếm' explained as 'không đủ cho mọi cách dùng có thể có'. Check clarity. 'Các cộng đồng cũng gặp sự khan hiếm' uses 'sự khan hiếm' as the glossary word.
read.sections.1.text.source: Usually, people do not have enough resources for everything they need and want. This problem is called scarcity. Scarcity does not mean there is nothing; it means there is not enough for every possible use. Noor's household shares one phone with a small amount of mobile data each week. Noor needs data for her online English class, and her cousins want to watch music videos. There is not enough data for both, so the household must decide. Communities face scarcity too. Hillside Learning Centre has one free room on Tuesday afternoons, so it must choose between a homework club and an art class.
read.sections.1.text.back: Usually, people do not have enough resources for everything they need and wish. This problem is called scarcity. Scarcity does not mean there is nothing at all; it means there is not enough for every possible way of using it. Noor's family shares one phone with a little mobile data each week. Noor needs the data for the online English class, while her younger cousins want to watch music videos. The data is not enough for both, so the whole family must decide. Communities also meet scarcity. Hillside Learning Centre has only one empty room on Tuesday afternoon, so it must choose between a homework club and an art class.

read.sections.1.simpler.note: 'Thường thì ta không có đủ ...' uses 'ta' (general 'we'); check it fits the register. The longest sentence is 21 syllables; consider splitting.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: Often there is not enough for all our needs and wants. This is called scarcity. It does not mean there is nothing. It means there is not enough for every use. Noor's home has one phone with a little data. Noor needs data for her class. Her cousins want music videos. There is not enough for both. So they must choose. A learning centre has one free room. It can hold a homework club or an art class, not both.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Usually we do not have enough for all essential needs and wishes. This is called scarcity. Scarcity does not mean having nothing. It means there is not enough for every use. Noor's home has one phone with little data. Noor needs data for the class. Her younger cousins want to watch music videos. The data is not enough for both. So the whole family must choose. A learning centre has one empty room. That room can be used for a homework club or an art class, not both.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Every choice has an opportunity cost
read.sections.2.heading.back: Every choice has an opportunity cost

read.sections.2.text.note: 'Chi phí cơ hội' defined as 'lựa chọn tốt nhất tiếp theo mà bạn bỏ đi'. 'chỗ ở' (space) in 'thời gian, sức lực, chỗ ở' may be misread as 'a place to live'; a reviewer should replace it with a word for 'room or space' (không gian, chỗ). | Review: 'chỗ ở' means housing/accommodation; English 'space' (e.g. a room). Meaning error. Native speaker: is 'không gian' clear for a 12-year-old, or would 'chỗ' / 'một căn phòng' be better? [Reviewer changed: sức lực, chỗ ở hoặc một cơ hội khác → sức lực, không gian hoặc một cơ hội khác]
read.sections.2.text.source: Whenever you choose one thing, you give up something else. The next-best option you give up is called the opportunity cost. On Saturday afternoon, Noor can play football with friends or practise English with a study partner. She chooses English, so her opportunity cost is the football game. Opportunity cost is not only about money; it can also be time, energy, space or another chance. Thinking about opportunity cost does not tell you which choice is correct. Instead, it helps you understand what you are giving up. Before deciding, ask: What do we need? What do we want? What will we give up?
read.sections.2.text.back: Each time you choose one thing, you must give up another. The next best choice that you throw away is called opportunity cost. On Saturday afternoon, Noor can play football with friends or practise English with a classmate. She chooses English, so her opportunity cost is the football match. Opportunity cost is not only about money; it can also be time, energy, living place (accommodation) or another opportunity. Thinking about opportunity cost does not tell you which choice is right. Instead, it helps you understand what you are giving up. Before deciding, ask: What do we need? What do we want? What will we give up?

read.sections.2.simpler.note: 'thời gian hay chỗ' for 'time or space'; same worry about 'chỗ'. | Review: 'chỗ' alone is vague (spot/seat); matched to standard text 'không gian'. [Reviewer changed: Nó cũng có thể là thời gian hay chỗ. → Nó cũng có thể là thời gian hay không gian.]
read.sections.2.simpler.source: When you choose one thing, you give up another. The best thing you did not pick is the opportunity cost. On Saturday, Noor can play football. Or she can practise English with a friend. She picks English. So the football game is her opportunity cost. Opportunity cost is not only about money. It can be time or space too. It does not tell you the right choice. It shows what you give up.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: When you choose one thing, you throw away another. The best thing that you do not choose is the opportunity cost. On Saturday, Noor can play football. Or she can practise English with a classmate. She chooses English. So the football match is her opportunity cost. Opportunity cost is not only about money. It can also be time or place/spot. It does not tell which choice is right. It shows what you are throwing away.

A reviewer should check the tone and the sentence 'Video cũng cho thấy thời gian cũng có thể là một cái giá phải trả' (repeated 'cũng'; may be reworded). | Review: Doubled 'cũng ... cũng' was stiff. watch.summary.source: This short video explains opportunity cost. When you pick one thing, you cannot have another. The next-best thing you give up is your opportunity cost. In the video, a young man called Mario needs a new phone. He also wants a new games console. His money is not enough for both, so he has to choose. He could buy a cheaper phone and get both things. But then his phone has fewer features. That is his opportunity cost. The video also shows that time can be a cost, not only money. It says the real cost of a choice is more than its price. Thinking about opportunity cost helps you compare needs and wants before you decide.
watch.summary.back: This short video explains opportunity cost. When you choose one thing, you cannot have another. The next best thing you throw away is your opportunity cost. In the video, a young man named Mario needs a new phone. He also wants a new game console. His money is not enough for both, so he must choose. He could buy a cheaper phone and have both things. But then his phone has fewer features. That is his opportunity cost. The video also shows that time can also be a price to pay, not only money. The video says the real price of a choice is bigger than its money price. Thinking about opportunity cost helps you compare essential needs and wishes before deciding.
